CausalChain: Overexpression of circMAT2B -> Upregulation/maintenance of oncogenic PKM2 activity (via microRNA sponging and/or protein interactions) -> Enhanced aerobic glycolysis and lactate production -> Acidification of tumor microenvironment stabilizes HIF-1α -> Promotion of angiogenesis, metastasis, and sorafenib resistance -> CRISPR-mediated inhibition of circMAT2B -> Disruption of circMAT2B-mediated miRNA/protein interactions -> Shift from PKM2-driven glycolysis to PKM1-like oxidative phosphorylation -> Reduced lactate production -> Destabilization of HIF-1α -> Decreased angiogenesis and metastasis -> Enhanced sorafenib sensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC, CRISPR-based inhibition of circMAT2B will specifically disrupt its regulatory interactions (including miRNA sponging and modulating protein-protein interactions) that support oncogenic PKM2 activity. This disruption will trigger a metabolic reprogramming from a glycolysis-dominant state to enhanced oxidative phosphorylation, thereby reducing lactate production. The consequent reduction in lactate concentrations is expected to diminish the acidification of the tumor microenvironment and destabilize HIF-1α, leading to decreased angiogenesis and metastatic potential. Collectively, these metabolic and microenvironmental changes will render tumors more responsive to sorafenib therapy. To validate this hypothesis, we will employ CRISPR genome editing alongside complementary RNA interference techniques to mitigate off-target effects, supported by advanced metabolic flux assays and multi-omics analyses that together will delineate the precise molecular interactions and metabolic shifts, while also accounting for parallel pathways such as mTOR-mediated glycolytic regulation.
Abstract: Recent studies in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) highlight complex regulatory networks involving non-coding RNAs and metabolic reprogramming. Here, we hypothesize that CRISPR-mediated inhibition of circMAT2B disrupts its modulation of oncogenic PKM2—normally maintained via microRNA sponging and protein‐protein interactions—thereby shifting cell metabolism from aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect) toward enhanced oxidative phosphorylation. This shift results in reduced lactate production, leading to destabilization of HIF-1α and subsequent inhibition of angiogenesis and metastasis, ultimately enhancing the efficacy of sorafenib. Our approach integrates state-of-the-art CRISPR tools with advanced metabolic flux assays and multi-omics analyses, while incorporating rigorous off-target controls and complementary RNA interference methods to validate the specificity of the observed effects. Furthermore, this strategy permits a re‐evaluation of parallel metabolic regulatory mechanisms, including contributions from mTOR-dependent signaling pathways, providing a comprehensive framework for targeted metabolic reprogramming in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on CRISPR-mediated circMAT2B inhibition leading to reduced PKM2 activity and a metabolic switch that lowers lactate production, thereby destabilizing HIF-1α to enhance sorafenib sensitivity. The revised hypothesis retains this core causal chain but explicitly refines the mechanistic details by emphasizing the disruption of circMAT2B’s miRNA sponging and protein-protein interactions. It further incorporates contemporary technologies such as rigorous off-target controls (including complementary RNA interference), advanced metabolic flux assays, and comprehensive multi-omics analyses to ensure a specific and detailed mapping of the metabolic reprogramming. Additionally, the revised hypothesis acknowledges the potential contribution of parallel pathways (e.g., mTOR signaling) in the regulation of glycolysis, thereby integrating existing literature observations and enhancing the practical implementability of the approach.
